name: Turkish Iskender Turkey Bowls
writer_notes: SELECTOR: Toasted pita cubes under spiced turkey, tomato-butter sauce and garlic yogurt - assembles in a tray and holds well. Verified source: full recipe, 4 servings, 482 cal / 10g protein. Confidence note: source protein is low because it is bread-and-butter heavy; our build shifts the ratio to turkey-forward. Distinct from any live gyro/doner bowl by the tomato-butter-yogurt sauce. | HARVEST: Source uses beef, not turkey. Served over pita, not rice. Published protein of 10g looks inconsistent with 500g of beef across 4 servings; treat source nutrition as suspect.
OVERRIDE Green Bell Peppers: WAVE-4: source grills a couple of long peppers as GARNISH; 4 full bells scaled to 14 was 1.7 kg - cut to 1 pepper at src scale
OVERRIDE Diced Tomatoes: WAVE-4: '2 tomatoes, quartered and grilled' fresh, not cans
OVERRIDE Beef Flank/Sirloin Steak: TITLE-PROTEIN SWAP: titled turkey; sliced flank -> sliced turkey breast, grams kept
intro_html: Iskender kebab is named for Iskender Efendi, the man in Bursa who supposedly turned the lamb spit sideways in the 1860s and changed Turkish cooking. The dish is sliced meat over toasted bread cubes, a bright tomato sauce poured across it, melted butter drizzled over that, and cool yogurt alongside. Each serving carries {{protein}} grams of protein and {{cal}} calories for about ${{cost_ps}} (at everyday cost). It is the most expensive plate in this group and the one most worth making when you want to eat something you cannot get locally.
cost_note_html: Real Omaha store prices from our weekly grocery board (2026). They still swing by store and by what is on sale.
cost_lines: Pantry seasonings (black pepper, salt, red pepper flakes, paprika): ~$0.80. From jars you keep on hand.

Batch total: about $38.39 across 14 servings, so roughly $2.74 per bowl. This counts only the amounts this batch actually uses from each package, so it is the cost of the food in the containers, not a register receipt.

True shopping cost: about $54.14 across 14 servings, roughly $3.87 per bowl. What the register trip looks like if your pantry is already stocked. Meat, produce, and packaged items are counted as the whole packages you have to buy, since you cannot grab a partial box, can, or jar. Pantry staples you already own (rice, seasonings, oils, and long-lasting sauces) are counted at only what this batch uses.

Starting with an empty pantry? Add about $9.86 one time. That is the extra cost of buying full containers of every pantry staple in this recipe instead of just the amounts used, which puts a first shopping trip near $64.00. Those containers then feed this batch and many more after it.
cost_closing_html: About ${{cost_ps}} a serving (at everyday cost). Turkey breast and a mountain of tomatoes and peppers push this to the top of the range. What you get for it is a dish most people have never had at home, built entirely out of grocery store items.
shop_smart: Two frozen turkey breast roasts cover this batch. Roast them, chill them completely, and then slice thin against the grain, which is far easier cold than warm.
Canned diced tomatoes are the base of the sauce and this recipe uses a lot of them. Store brand blends down identically and goes on sale by the case.

Green peppers cost less than any other color and get charred here, which is the traditional garnish for Iskender. If your store carries Turkish or Anaheim long peppers at a similar price, those are closer to the original.
Greek yogurt in the 32 oz tub costs far less per ounce than the single-serve cups. The tub also keeps for weeks, so nothing goes to waste.
make_it: Weigh your empty mixing pot and write the number down for portioning later.
Cut the tortillas into bite-sized squares, spread them on a sheet pan, and toast at 375F for 8 to 10 minutes until dry and lightly golden. They need to be dry enough to hold up under sauce.
Char the green peppers whole under the broiler for 8 to 10 minutes, turning once, until the skins blister, then slice them into strips.

Heat most of the olive oil in a large skillet and cook the sliced onion for 6 minutes, then add the tomato paste, paprika, red pepper flakes, salt, and black pepper and cook two minutes until the paste darkens.
Add the canned diced tomatoes and simmer 20 to 25 minutes until the sauce reduces and thickens enough to hold its shape on a spoon.
Sear the sliced turkey breast in the remaining olive oil over high heat in batches, just long enough to get color on the edges without drying it out.
Whisk the Greek yogurt smooth with a pinch of salt and a splash of water so it pours rather than sits in a lump.

Build the bowls: toasted bread cubes on the bottom, seared turkey over them, the simmered sauce spooned across, melted butter drizzled over the top, charred peppers on the side, and the yogurt in its own corner.
portion_html: Weigh the bread, turkey, and sauce together, subtract your empty pot weight, and divide by 14, then keep the yogurt in a separate small container for each bowl. Building the base to a weight is what keeps the bread-to-meat ratio honest. Each serving comes to {{cal}} calories and {{protein}} grams of protein.

steps: Cut the tortillas into squares and toast at 375F for 8 to 10 minutes until dry.
Char the green peppers under the broiler until blistered, then slice into strips.
Cook the onion in olive oil, add the tomato paste, paprika, red pepper flakes, salt, and pepper, then the diced tomatoes, and simmer 20 to 25 minutes.
Sear the sliced turkey breast in batches over high heat, and whisk the Greek yogurt smooth with salt.
Layer bread, turkey, the simmered sauce, and melted butter, add peppers and yogurt on the side, and portion into 14 containers.
